Rudolph remained modernist; his emphasis on personal effort does not constitute rejection of modernism. Rudolph's philosophy is clearly articulated and consistent; personal effort and spatial drama were his consistent commitments. Rudolph as representing a modernist position that privileges individual architectural authorship, emphasizing 'the importance of direct control over design without excessive bureaucratic mediation.' This contrasts with Gropius's workshop collectivity and Le Corbusier's systematized mass-production approaches—different modernist answers to how design should be organized and controlled.
